title: Next.js Routing
description: File-system routing, middleware, and parallel routes in Next.js.

data.text: Next.js App Router uses file-system routing. Folders and files define routes, layouts, and loading states.

data.code:
app/
  layout.tsx
  page.tsx
  about/
    page.tsx
  dashboard/
    layout.tsx
    page.tsx
    settings/
      page.tsx
data.title: App Router directory structure
Parallel Routes
data.text: Next.js supports multiple pages in the same layout using @folder naming.

Next.js derives routes from the file system: a folder is a path segment and `page.tsx` is the component served at that path. A folder wrapped in brackets such as `[id]` is a dynamic segment, and `[slug]` inside `[...slug]` catches multiple segments. Layouts nest around pages.

data.title: An App Router page and layout

data.text: Special files next to a page wire up the surrounding states without extra code: `loading.tsx` renders while a server component waits, `error.tsx` renders when it throws, and `not-found.tsx` renders for an unmatched route. `route.ts` defines a server-side HTTP handler at a URL.

data.title: A loading boundary and a route handler
Interview angle: server components and the URL
data.text: The key difference from a client-side router is that Next.js resolves the route on the server. A server component can read the URL through `params` and `searchParams` and fetch data directly, so there is no client-side loader. Mention that layouts are not re-rendered on navigation within the same layout, which is why shared UI and providers belong there.

terms.definition: Folder in parentheses without affecting URL.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Route groups organize without affecting URLs.
